blocks.prompt: The Needle That Knows Which Way Is North
blocks.text: A compass has one job. It shows you which way is north. The trick is hidden inside. The needle is a magnet. It is painted red on one end. Earth is a giant magnet too. The needle feels Earth pulling on it, so it swings until it lines up. Then it stops and points north. It does this in the dark. It does this in the fog. It does this in the middle of the ocean, where every wave looks the same. Turn the compass around and the needle does not care. It swings right back to north.

blocks.prompt: How a Compass Finds North
blocks.text: Deep inside Earth, far below the ground you walk on, there is a ball of iron. Some of it is solid and some of it is melted, and the melted part is always moving. All that moving metal turns our planet into a giant magnet. You cannot see it or feel it, but it is there, wrapped around the whole world. A compass needle is a small magnet too. It sits on a sharp point so it can spin freely. Because magnets pull on other magnets, the needle swings until it lines up with Earth's field. One end settles pointing north. The other end points south. Then it stops, and it stays that way until you move it. The first compasses were made in China more than two thousand years ago. They were not for travel. People carved a spoon out of lodestone, a rock that is magnetic all by itself, and spun it on a smooth board to help make decisions. Hundreds of years later, sailors figured out the better use. With a needle, a ship could keep going the right way even when clouds hid the sun and the stars.

blocks.prompt: Why the Needle Lies a Little
blocks.text: A compass looks simple. A needle, a dial, a ring of letters. What it is actually doing is reading a machine the size of a planet. About eighteen hundred miles beneath your feet, Earth's outer core is molten iron, hot enough to glow and heavy enough to sink. That liquid metal churns and swirls as the planet spins, and moving metal makes a magnetic field. Scientists call the whole arrangement the geodynamo. Its field reaches out through the rock, past the ocean, and into space, and your compass needle is small enough and free enough to feel it. Here is the part that surprises people. Your compass does not point to the North Pole. It points to the magnetic north pole, which is a different place, and that place will not sit still. It has been wandering across the Arctic for as long as anyone has measured it, drifting out of northern Canada and heading toward Siberia, some years by more than twenty five miles. Mapmakers have to keep up. The gap between true north and magnetic north is called declination, and it changes depending on where you stand. In Maine the needle leans west of true north. In Oregon it leans east. Somewhere in between there is a line where the needle happens to be right, and even that line slides across the country over time. So a compass is honest but not exact. Every serious navigator learns the same lesson: trust the needle, then correct it.

blocks.prompt: The Machine at the Center of the World
blocks.text: Pick up a compass and you are holding one end of a conversation. The other end is roughly two thousand miles below you, and it is made of liquid iron. Earth's outer core is a shell of molten metal wrapped around a solid inner core. It is under crushing pressure and it never stops moving. Heat rising from below, the planet's spin, and the slow freezing of the inner core all stir it, and because iron carries electric current, that churning generates a magnetic field. Physicists call the process the geodynamo. The field it produces leaks out through eighteen hundred miles of rock, spreads around the planet, and keeps going far into space, where it deflects the stream of charged particles the sun throws at us. Your compass needle, floating in its little pool of fluid, is reading the edge of that machine. The reading comes with conditions. First, magnetic north is not true north, and the difference, called declination, is different in every place and changes every year. Second, the field does not lie flat. It dives into the ground, steeply near the poles and gently near the equator, so compass needles are weighted by region to keep them level. Take a compass made for Alaska down to Ecuador and the needle will tilt and drag. Third, the needle answers any magnet, not just the planet. A phone, a speaker, a steel belt buckle, an engine block: hold any of them close and the needle will happily point at the wrong thing. Steel ships were such a problem that navigators bolted iron balls beside the compass to cancel the ship's own pull. And the field itself is not permanent. Iron grains locked in ancient lava record the direction the field faced when the rock cooled, and those records show something startling. The field has reversed hundreds of times. North and south trade places. The last full flip was about seven hundred and eighty thousand years ago. It will happen again, though nobody can say when. Humans built a needle to read this field. Other animals did not have to. Sea turtles, robins, and salmon all appear to sense it directly, using it to find beaches and rivers they have not visited in years. We invented the compass. They were born with one.

notes: Outer core: liquid iron and nickel, about 1,800 miles down
Geodynamo: moving metal makes a self-sustaining field

Declination differs at every point and every year
Last full magnetic reversal: about 780,000 years ago

blocks.prompt: The Honest Lie: What a Compass Is Actually Telling You
blocks.text: Every compass tells a small lie, and every good navigator knows it. That is not a flaw in the tool. It is a fact about the planet. Start underneath. About eighteen hundred miles below your shoes, the rock gives way to Earth's outer core: a shell of liquid iron and nickel at temperatures approaching those at the surface of the sun, wrapped around a solid inner core roughly the size of Pluto. That liquid never rests. Heat escapes upward, the inner core slowly freezes and releases lighter material, and the planet's rotation twists the whole flow into columns. Moving metal carries electric current, electric current makes magnetism, and magnetism in a spinning conductor sustains itself. The arrangement is called the geodynamo, and it is the only reason a compass has anything to talk to. The field it throws off surrounds the planet and extends tens of thousands of miles into space, where it turns aside the charged particles streaming off the sun. Without it, that stream would have stripped away much of our atmosphere long ago. The needle in your hand is reading the far edge of a self-sustaining engine you will never see. Now the lie. The needle does not point at the North Pole. It points at the magnetic north pole, and the two are hundreds of miles apart. Worse, the magnetic pole moves. Through most of the twentieth century it crept across Arctic Canada at roughly nine miles a year. Then, around the 1990s, it accelerated past thirty, sprinting toward Siberia so quickly that the agencies who publish the world magnetic model issued an early update in 2019, ahead of the scheduled release, because aircraft and phones were leaning on numbers already going stale. The angle between true north and magnetic north is called declination. It is different at every point on Earth, and different every year at the same point. This is why a topographic map prints a declination diagram in its margin, and why the number printed there has an expiration date. The complications compound. Earth's field does not run flat along the ground. It dips into it, nearly vertical near the poles, nearly horizontal at the equator, so manufacturers counterweight needles for particular latitude zones. A compass bought in Norway sulks in Peru. The needle also cannot tell your planet from your pocket: speakers, phones, car doors, and the steel bars inside concrete all pull on it. Iron ships pulled so hard that navigators mounted spheres of soft iron on either side of the compass housing to cancel the vessel's own magnetism, and sailors still call those spheres Kelvin's balls. And the field is not even loyal. Lava cools with its iron grains frozen in the direction the field faced that day, which hands geologists a written record going back millions of years. It says the poles have swapped hundreds of times. The last complete reversal was about 780,000 years ago. During a flip the field weakens, wanders, and may briefly show several poles at once. Any compass alive for that would be worthless. So why do we still trust it? Because a compass is honest about what it is doing. It reports the local field, always, in fog, in darkness, in a snowstorm, with no batteries and no satellites. Everything that makes it inexact is knowable and correctable. You look up your declination. You buy the right zone. You keep the steel away. A satellite receiver is more precise and less trustworthy, because when it fails it can fail silently. The compass never pretends. It just requires you to know something. That was true for a Song dynasty sailor watching a magnetized needle float on a bowl of water nine hundred years ago, and it is true for a hiker on a ridge tonight.
